source.author: verg
source.text: Nec non et vario noctem sermone trahebat infelix Dido, longumque bibebat amorem, multa super Priamo rogitans, super Hectore multa; nunc quibus Aurorae venisset filius armis, nunc quales Diomedis equi, nunc quantus Achilles.
source.text_original: Nec non et vario noctem sermone trahebat / infelix Dido, longumque bibebat amorem, / multa super Priamo rogitans, super Hectore multa; / nunc quibus Aurorae venisset filius armis, / nunc quales Diomedis equi, nunc quantus Achilles.
source.text_english: And also unhappy Dido kept drawing out the night with varied conversation and kept drinking in love for long, asking many things about Priam, many things about Hector; now about what arms Aurora’s son had come with, now what Diomedes’ horses were like, now how great Achilles was.

reuse.author: val
reuse.text: Thracius hie noctem dulci testudine vates extrahit, ut steterit redimitus tempora vittis Phrixus et iniustas contectus nubibus aras fugerit Inoo linquens Athamanta Learcho; aureus ut iuvenem miserantibus intulit undis vector et astrictis ut sedit cornibus Helle.
reuse.text_original: Thracius hie noctem dulci testudine vates / extrahit, ut steterit redimitus tempora vittis / Phrixus et iniustas contectus nubibus aras / fugerit Inoo linquens Athamanta Learcho; / aureus ut iuvenem miserantibus intulit undis / vector et astrictis ut sedit cornibus Helle.
reuse.text_english: Here the Thracian singer passes the night with his sweet lyre, as Phrixus stood with his temples bound with fillets and, covered by the clouds, fled the unjust altars, leaving Athamas and Learcho for Ino; as the golden one bore the youth on the pitying waves, and as Helle sat upon the clasped horns.
